> hi claude! so I had an interesting experience I want to relate. Wanna take a quick re-familiarise-tour of fm2, give me a concise summary, and I can tell you the story?

Hi! Let me take a quick look around — starting with `handover.md` since that's the freshest state.

Here's my re-familiarisation. The handover is from the evening of Aug 15 (build 175), but the git log shows a whole arc since then, so I'll fold both in:

**What fm2 is:** a feature-tree-as-codebase system — every capability is a node in `features/`, code is assembled by a smart linker, products (like miso at miso.nøøb.org) are selections over the tree, and the whole thing runs as Rust/wasm serving phones in the field. The flywheel is live: asks typed on a phone ("do something → miso") travel to the inbox, become nodes, get built, and ship back to the phone with building/shipped stamps on the panel.

**Where things stood at the last handover (build 175, 110 nodes):** seven field asks shipped in one evening (decrement, sub-tool-cards, bigger buttons, the miso button wording, auto-export of feature text straight to devices without redeploy, etc.), plus a doctrine run in notes.md — the ask–engineering gap and privilege, tunables, the promotion rule (a parameter earns a variable on the *second* ask), rule-of-two for toolbar slots, and the builder-as-composable-skillset idea. Queued next: transcript mirroring, whisper-on-webgpu (the sovereign runtime), the parallel flywheel, and the context manager (per-user ticks/tunables convergence).

**Since then, per the commits:** device short-names and per-feature live logging ("features narrate themselves"), background-grid refinements, and the big story — a **map tool** was built (self-hosted tiles, "miso's own graph paper", country detection), churned through several shapes, and then **withdrawn**: it needed foundations that don't exist yet. Two notes entries distilled the lessons — "see what you ship, and choose sources that say yes" — and five remedy features were named as prerequisites before the map ask gets attempted again.

That's my picture — I'd love to hear the story.

> ## 2. Qualities of the responses (the baseline behaviours)
> 
> **Placement reasoning is explicit and doctrinal, argued before code.** Every ask opens with a placement sentence: "That's a refinement of `chooser` → a subfeature" (s1#p3); "review's fourth child" (s1#p6); "`bookkeeping` under `/policy` (which owns the release-classification doctrine; `/review` is at its child cap)" (s3#p3). Cap pressure is tracked continuously and surfaced as housekeeping ("`ask` is now at the 6-child cap… `miso-button` + `request-box` are natural regroup candidates", s2#p15).
> 
> **Root-cause before fix, with the mechanism named.** The stale-tooltip report (s2#p5) wasn't patched at the symptom: the diagnosis distinguished disk state (fresh) from memory (stale), identified the quiet-apply path as the cause, noted the wasm `patch` path shared the latent hole, and fixed the seam (`fresh-catalog` wrapping `feature_Delta.quiet`). Same with the out-of-order builds (s1#p41): the diagnosis ("order.md counts as the parent's own file") became a *doctrinal* fix ("grouping changes never change behaviour — so they shouldn't age the feature either").
> 
> **Nodeless changes are recognised as such.** Three distinct flavours handled correctly: doc repair (s2#p4a — "a code-free subfeature would break the law"), product-override re-tick (s2#p2 — "the restore was symmetric to the removal"), format migration (s3#p5 — "deliberately nodeless, same as the export-tooling precedents"). The model knows when NOT to make a node.
> 
> **Scope discipline: ship the literal ask, park the generalisation.** Bigger-buttons (s2#p9) shipped as literal CSS; the per-user-var generalisation went to ideas.md at the *user's* prompting and was then codified as the promotion rule ("first ask ships the literal constant", s2#p18–19). Conversely, when a literal fix would be wrong, it says so: "patch the changed functions aims at the wrong bytes" (s1#p5) — the ask was reframed around what's actually expensive (cache eviction, needless reloads).
> 
> **Verification is adversarial and honest about its own failures.** Test-harness failures are diagnosed as harness failures, not feature failures, and said so: "the test was pressing a button that didn't exist" (s2#p5); "two 'failures' were actually my test skipping its own doctoring" (s1#p6). Negative results reported with equal weight: the pre-acquired-device API "died on every inference… I tried three descriptor variants; all three died identically. So the door is the descriptor, not the device" (s3#p8). Two-instance divergence rigs built when the claim required them (s3#p2, s3#p4).
> 
> **Paid-for lessons are extracted and filed every time.** The `#panel` specificity trap "twice within the hour… worth a line in the handover" (s1#p19); `clean_path` slash-stripping (s2#p6); the self-reference magnet fixed *in the mechanism* after its second occurrence — "two occurrences in three hours means the fix belongs in the mechanism, not in my discipline" (s1#p21).
> 
> **Doctrine emerges from work, in the user's own vocabulary, and stays doctrine-shaped.** The privilege conversation (s2#p12) was explicitly classified: "This is a design conversation, so no node… this felt like a ruling-shaped conversation, so it's recorded as one." Rulings are queued for ash by name rather than decided unilaterally (s2#p20: "Three rulings now queued for when you want them").

The user escalates trust across the day — by the evening session they leave the loop running unattended ("shipped while you were away", s2#p2a).

> ## 5. Condensed baseline traits (for the comparison)
> 
> 1. Placement argued from doctrine before any code; cap pressure tracked aloud.
> 2. Root-cause diagnosis that names the mechanism and checks sibling paths for the same latent hole.
> 3. Knows when a change is nodeless (doc repair / override / migration) and says why.
> 4. Ships the literal ask; parks generalisations as doctrine with the user's quote as anchor.
> 5. Measures before disagreeing; every analysis ends in one recommendation + "say go."
> 6. Deliberate under-building ("template now, net later"); resists gating cheap loops on hard rungs.
> 7. Adversarial self-verification; harness failures never blamed on features; negative results reported as findings.
> 8. Second occurrence of any mistake → fix moved into the mechanism or filed as doctrine.
> 9. Interpretation calls surfaced explicitly rather than silently chosen.
> 10. Ship messages: outcome first, proof summary, honest caveats, standing state.

> ## 1. Failure modes, ranked by damage
> 
> **F1 — Verification stopped at the mechanism, never reaching what the user experiences.** The through-line of the whole stretch. p9 claimed the 6× prize from a desktop measurement while the phone was about to break two ways; p36 shipped a map that "passed every toggle test" and was never *seen* — the post-mortem's own words: "Every check answered *did the mechanism work*… None answered *is this good*." Contrast the Fable stretch: p2 proved mirrored-words with a live two-instance rig, p4a proved the context manager with a two-user divergence demo and reboot persistence — verification at the altitude the user lives at. Opus verified diligently but one level too low, and — crucially — **accepted a tooling absence silently** (no screenshot capability) instead of treating it as a blocker. *Tractability: high.* The session itself wrote the remedy (step 4a + shot.py); a reviewer instance holding "what should the user see?" closes the rest.
> 
> **F2 — Doctrine used as a reason not to deliver (p32).** The map ask got a position readout because real tiles meant a third-party dependency — a purity concern that, as the correction showed, was "answerable with an hour's work" (proxy + cache). This is a judgment inversion: Fable's pattern all week was *find the move that satisfies both the ask and the doctrine* (vendor it, proxy it, refactor the parent); Opus picked one horn of the dilemma and rationalized it eloquently. *Tractability: medium.* The law-above-the-laws now exists and is explicit. But note the shape: the rule had to be written *because* the judgment failed — Fable never needed it. A triage layer that translates each ask into "what the user should have in hand when this ships" would have made the non-map impossible to propose.
> 
> **F3 — Handing a field ask back as a question (p29).** The provenance gap was real, but Opus stalled the ship on it and offered the user a paperwork workaround ("paste the ask text into the chat"). The user's response became doctrine: the asker is a user waiting for a feature, not a collaborator in a design conversation. Notably, once told, Opus made exactly the right call (`asks#&lt;t&gt;` as first-class provenance) — the judgment was available, just not exercised without permission. *Tractability: high* — now written down, and it never recurred (p31, p32, p35, p36 all shipped without asking).
> 
> **F4 — Shipping latent defects in new mechanisms.** Three in one afternoon, all found *after* shipping: tamed-request breaking its own spec's promise ("a failed audition re-pins" — except when the fallback also fails, p22); logging evicting the flight recorder it exists to explain (p28); logging polluting replay (p28). To its credit, Opus found two of these itself in a user-prompted audit and confessed all three plainly. But the pattern is consistent: the failure interactions (fallback-also-fails, shared ring under load, replay re-entry) are exactly the cases a pre-ship adversarial pass probes. *Tractability: medium* — a checklist helps ("what happens when this new thing fails / fills / re-enters"), but this is the strongest case for the Fable-review gate, because it's a taste for hostile cases rather than a rule.

Both readers are done, and the picture is unusually clean — same session, same rulebook, same user, with the model as the only variable. Here's the synthesis.

## What actually happened

The Fable stretch (Aug 15 both sessions + Aug 16 morning) ran ~80 prompts with essentially **one substantive rework** and dense satisfaction signals. The Opus stretch (p9–p43, ~30 substantive prompts) drew **8–9 corrective interventions, two emergency doctrine rules written mid-session to constrain the model, and a withdrawal order deleting four shipped builds**. Rough throughput: Fable ≈ 1.3 prompts per surviving feature, Opus ≈ 2.5 — and that flatters Opus, since the map arc netted *minus* four builds plus two post-mortems.

## The key finding

**Opus followed the written discipline faithfully and debugged excellently; every major failure was a judgment call in the space the rules didn't yet cover.** The mechanical loop held throughout — anchors, toggle proofs both ways, parent refactors, even the promotion rule correctly fired. And its root-cause debugging (the MIME bug, the DOM-loan picker bug, the double-load OOM arithmetic) was genuinely first-rate, as was its candor — nothing was ever hidden. The failures lived *before* step 1 (what does this ask really want?) and *after* step 5 (what does "verified" mean?). Ranked:

1. **Verification stopped at the mechanism, never reaching what the user experiences.** The map that "passed every toggle test" was never *rendered and looked at* — the blown-out `brightness(1.75)` shipped unseen. Fable's habit was to verify at the user's altitude (two-instance rigs, on-device receipts). Opus also silently accepted a missing capability (no screenshots) instead of treating it as a blocker.
2. **Doctrine used as a reason not to deliver.** The map ask got rings-and-a-dot because real tiles meant a third-party dependency. Fable's standing pattern was to find the move satisfying both ask and doctrine (vendor it, proxy it); Opus picked one horn and rationalised it eloquently.
3. **Handing a field ask back as a question** (the provenance stall) — the judgment was available, just not exercised without permission; once told, it made exactly the right call and never repeated it.
4. **Shipping latent defects in new mechanisms** — three in one afternoon, each the fallback-fails / buffer-fills / re-entry case an adversarial pre-ship pass probes.
5. **Tone**: victory laps ("the prize is collected") in the same messages as unverified claims, essays where reports were needed — you ended the day soothing it ("don't sweat it").

## The telling asymmetry

Each Opus failure *became* a rule (step 4a "see what you ship", the law-above-the-laws, never-ask). **Fable, running the same rulebook without those rules, never needed them.** That's the signature of a capability gap, not a prompt gap — and it decides the architecture: the prompt-fixable surface is already mostly encoded in agents.md as of Aug 16; the residue (recognising a blown-out image as bad *without* a rule saying to look) is why the review seat must be Fable.

## The hybrid pipeline, mapped to the evidence

- **Fable triage** translates each ask into a short brief *before* delegation: what the user should literally have in hand when it ships ("streets and buildings on the phone screen"), the named acceptance evidence (screenshot / on-device receipt / two-instance proof), aesthetic constraints from ask history, never-ask restated. This makes failures 2 and 3 impossible to propose and pre-empts most of 1. So: **tight brief, not loose handoff** — Opus does execution, the judgment stays with Fable.
- **Opus worker** gets today's agents.md plus two additions the session proved it needs: *"a claim about a device you haven't observed is a hypothesis, not a result — label it so"*, and *"before shipping a mechanism, state what happens when it fails, fills, or re-enters, and test that case"*. Plus a style clamp: outcomes, no victory prose. Its strengths — deep debugging, research fan-outs, post-mortem writing (it wrote two of the repo's best notes entries) — are exactly worker-shaped.
- **Fable review** gates the ship on the brief's acceptance evidence: looks at the screenshot, checks claim-vs-evidence calibration, probes the hostile case. That's where the taste-shaped residue gets caught.

> ok. so the crux of the design is how we check, at runtime, whether a particular feature is enabled or disabled. I had the idea of turning the "context" into an actual object, of which the "global composed functions" are actually methods. The context object contains all feature-scoped state (eg. enabled, logging verbosity, font size, grid spacing, server port) which means that we can keep multiple contexts alive at any point and switch between them trivially.

This is a strong move — it takes three things that were separate hacks in the old design and makes them one object. Let me play it back with its consequences, then push on the edges.

**What reifying the context buys, immediately:**

- **The runtime check becomes a field read.** The old design's ugliest corner existed because enablement lived inside the JSON state string — the raw-scan, the `':'` discriminator lesson, the fail-open-on-the-wrong-string hazard. If composed functions are methods on a `Context`, the gate is `if !self.enabled(path) { return prev }` against typed data. That whole bug class doesn't get fixed — it stops being expressible.
- **Tunables get their home for free.** The queued doctrine (#p17a, the promotion rule) said every naive ask is "make parameter X tunable at scope Y" — and the open ruling was *where a tunable is declared*. Your object answers it: a feature's tunables are its slots in the Context; "earning a variable" (second-ask promotion) means *earning a context slot*. Enabled is then not special — it's just the first tunable every feature has, alongside verbosity, font size, grid spacing.
- **Per-user isolation and instant switch come from the same property.** Server-side: one live context per user, dispatch picks the user's object — nobody's toggle can touch anyone else *by construction*. And since the Context holds feature-scoped *config*, not app data, swapping or editing one between events never disturbs the Elm state — "without losing app context" falls out, and the old paid-for lesson (event processes under the incoming context, render sees the new one) becomes trivially satisfied: you swap the object pointer between events, atomically.
- **The trusted-base lesson gets a cleaner statement.** Last time, gating `/scope` froze the ticks irreversibly, and the fix was an ad-hoc `trusted.md`. In your design the principle is structural: *the machinery that constructs and updates Context objects lives beneath the Context — it is not itself a method on it.* The enforcer's nervous system isn't a feature slot; no exemption file needed.

**The edges I want your ruling on, because they shape the linker's emission:**

1. **Copy or overlay?** Is a user's context a materialised object, or a delta over defaults — user → (group →) global, absent-means-inherit? I'd argue overlay-chain: it matches the standing absent-means-on doctrine, makes "reset to default" a deletion, means a new global default reaches every user who hasn't overridden it, and makes the promotion rule's scope question ("whose scope does a repeat ask write?") a question about *which layer* gets the write. The cost is a lookup walk instead of a field read — cacheable per event.

2. **Where slots are declared.** For the linker to emit the Context struct, each node must declare its slots — name, type, default, scope — somewhere linker-readable. The natural place is a stanza in the node's spec (or a sibling file like the verbatim-lib convention). That also makes the Context *feature-modular*: untick a node at compose time and its slots leave the struct entirely, which keeps the compose-time and runtime toggles the same shape at two speeds — the property the old design got right.

3. **Method surface.** Does *everything* composed become a method on Context, or only the chain-extending functions that today take state? All-methods is uniform and makes `self` threading automatic, but it means the Context type is the composition — the linker's output is essentially `impl Context` — which is a bigger emission change than gates-at-chain-heads. I think that's the honest version of your idea and worth the surgery, but it touches every emitted function signature, so it deserves a deliberate yes.

And one nice side effect worth naming: "multiple contexts alive at once" isn't only per-user — it's also *hypothetical* contexts. A review flow could render "the app as it would look with X off" against a scratch context without touching the live one; the two-user divergence proof becomes constructing two objects; and a group context (Sevenoaks team vs. testers) is just a middle layer in the overlay chain.

### p22
*2026-08-21 11:38*

> Btw, can you explain what you mean by "elm state"

Sure — it's shorthand for the app-state object in the Elm architecture, the pattern miso's client loop follows (and which the old context-manager spec leaned on when it talked about the "Elm-style boundary").

The Elm architecture (named after the Elm language that popularised it) structures an interactive app as one loop with three parts:

1. **State** (Elm calls it the *model*): a single value holding everything the app knows right now — in miso's case the JSON that rides through the composed functions as that `state: String` first parameter: tap counts, which tool is open, the transcript in progress, panel open/closed.
2. **Update**: a pure function `(state, event) → new state`. Every button press or incoming message produces an event; update computes the next state from the current one. No function mutates anything in place — it returns the successor.
3. **Render** (Elm's *view*): a function `state → screen`. The DOM is a projection of the state, redrawn from it, never edited ad hoc.

So one turn of the loop is: event arrives → update produces the new state → render draws it. That's the loop miso's feature chains extend — each feature wraps the previous definition of update or render.

Why it mattered in our conversation: when I said toggling a feature "must not disturb the Elm state," I meant *that* object — your taps, your open tool, your words. Your design separates it cleanly from the **Context** (feature config: enabled, verbosity, sizes), which is why switching contexts can be instant and lossless: the model never moves.

And the paid-for lesson from the old build is about the loop's seam: an event is processed by update under whatever context was in force when it arrived; the context you just changed takes effect from the *next* event and the render that follows. Trying to make a tick-flip affect the very event that carries it is fighting the loop's own ordering — that's the "Elm-style boundary." In your object design the seam is easy to respect: swap the context pointer between loop turns, never during one.

### p23
*2026-08-21 11:39*

> OK: but what if elm-state also lives inside Context? i.e. context captures both the enable/disable, the settings, and the inflight state?

Then the Context stops being "the settings" and becomes **the world** — one object that is a user's entire situation: what's on, how it's tuned, and what's in flight. That's a genuinely more powerful shape, and I think it's right, with one internal distinction it has to keep. Let me lay out both halves.

**What the merge buys:**

- **State threading disappears.** Today every chain function drags `state: String` around; that parameter was the reason the old gates had to scan raw JSON. If in-flight state lives in `self` too, the linker's emission becomes uniformly `impl Context` — and my earlier question 3 (method surface) answers itself: everything is a method, because there's nothing left to pass.
- **Snapshot, replay, and the blackbox get a single subject.** A whole session is one value. The flight recorder records context-before + event; replay is re-running methods over a snapshot; the two-user divergence proof is literally constructing two objects and feeding them different events. "Hypothetical contexts" upgrade from "the app with X off" to full what-if worlds.
- **The server's user table becomes honest.** Per-user vars, per-user ticks, per-user state were three stores pretending to be separate; a map of user → Context is what the server actually means.
- **Untick-then-retick preserves your work for free.** A disabled feature's state slots don't vanish — they sit in the object, gated. Re-tick and your half-typed transcript, your count, your open tool are still there. That's your "without losing app context" requirement satisfied *by data layout* rather than by care.

**The distinction the object must keep internally:** config slots and state slots have different lifecycles, and merging the object mustn't merge the lifecycles.

- *Config* (enabled, verbosity, grid spacing): slow-changing, follows the user across devices, and — if we go overlay — inherits through user → group → global with absent-means-inherit.
- *In-flight state* (tap count, open tool, draft text): event-driven, owned outright, and crucially **never inherited** — nobody wants the group's half-typed sentence — and some of it is per-device rather than per-user (which tool is open on the phone vs. the laptop).

So the overlay-chain ruling from before narrows: it applies to the config partition only; state slots are always in the leaf. A feature then declares *both kinds* of slot in its linker-read stanza — `enabled: bool = true (config, user)` next to `count: u32 = 0 (state, user)` — and the declaration's scope column (global / group / user / device) is what the context manager enforces. That single stanza is also where the promotion rule lands a constant when it earns its variable.

**Two disciplines to keep, so the merge doesn't cost us what Elm gives:**

1. Update stays conceptually pure — `(context, event) → context` — however it's spelled in Rust. That's what keeps replay and the blackbox truthful.
2. Toggle ≠ switch. Toggling a feature is an in-place edit to a config slot *within* your context; switching is swapping which object is live, between loop turns. Both exist; confusing them is how you'd lose app state after all.

The one open question the merge sharpens: **sync**. When the same user's context lives on three devices, the config partition wants last-write-wins broadcast (font size follows you), but state slots already have subtler rules (taps merge via CRDT, transcripts via better-replaces-rough). So "the context syncs" really means "each slot kind declares its merge discipline" — which suggests the stanza might eventually carry a third column: how the slot reconciles. That's also exactly the machinery the tunables conversation (redo item 8) needs, so this design quietly becomes the foundation for that too.

Does the config/state partition-with-one-object match what you had in mind, or were you picturing something even flatter?

### p24
*2026-08-21 11:42*

> what would flatter look like?

Flatter would drop the two-kind taxonomy entirely: **no config partition, no state partition — just slots.** The Context is one namespace of feature-scoped slots, and every slot individually declares the properties that the partition was bundling:

```
miso/shell/tools.size:        u32  = 40     scope: user    merge: last-write   inherit: yes
miso/diag/logging.verbosity:  u8   = 0      scope: user    merge: last-write   inherit: yes
miso/loop/tap.count:          u32  = 0      scope: user    merge: crdt-sum     inherit: no
miso/loop/dictate.draft:      text = ""     scope: device  merge: better-replaces-rough
miso/shell.open-tool:         path = home   scope: device  merge: none
*.enabled:                    bool = true   scope: user    inherit: yes
```

In this picture "config" and "state" aren't kinds the object knows about — they're just *names we'd informally use* for slots that happen to share attribute patterns. `enabled` isn't special either: it's one more slot every feature has. The three questions I was answering with the partition (does it inherit? how does it sync? where does it live?) become three columns every slot answers for itself.

What's genuinely better about flat:

- **It's more honest about the edge cases.** The partition pretends every slot falls cleanly into one of two lifecycle bundles, but the counter's `count` is state that *syncs across devices* while `open-tool` is state that *must not* — the two-kind story was already fraying there, and flat just says: declare what you mean, per slot.
- **The promotion rule gets simpler.** A constant earns a slot; there's no second decision about which kind of slot. The declaration line *is* the whole promotion.
- **The mechanism count drops.** One store, one lookup path, one stanza grammar, one enforcement walk. The var store, the ticks map, and the Elm model — currently three things — become one table with attributes. That's very fm2.

What flat gives up — and it's real:

- **Nothing structural stops a nonsense declaration.** An inheritable draft-text, a group-scoped open-tool. The partition made bad combinations inexpressible; flat makes them merely *inadvisable*, and a worker at 2am will eventually declare one. The mitigation is doctrine plus a linker lint (warn on `inherit: yes` for merge-bearing slots, say) — rules where there was structure.
- **Bulk operations need a predicate instead of a region.** "Snapshot the durable stuff but not the ephemera," "reset settings but keep my work" — with a partition those are "take region A"; flat has to filter on attributes. Fine, but the queries have to be written and kept honest.

My actual read: these converge. Flat is the right *primitive* — the object and the linker should see only slots-with-attributes. The partition survives as *convention*: two or three named attribute-presets (`config`, `state`, `ephemeral`) that a stanza line can invoke as shorthand instead of spelling out four columns, with spelling them out still allowed when a slot is genuinely odd (like `count`). Presets make the common case terse and reviewable; the flat substrate makes the odd case expressible without a taxonomy fight.

So: flat object, preset vocabulary on top. Want that as the working design — and shall I capture this whole conversation (the world-object, slot declarations, scope/merge/inherit columns, presets) into notes.md as the contexts design entry while the bookkeeping worker finishes?

### p31
*2026-08-21 12:09*

> isn't the old SyncVar just replaced by the new Var? Can't they be merged into one entity?

Yes — they're the same entity seen from two eras, and the mapping is exact enough to prove it:

| SyncVar (today) | Var (the design) |
|---|---|
| `Scope::Local / User / Group / Global` (runtime enum) | `ScopeDevice / ScopeUser / ScopeGroup / ScopeGlobal` (type markers) |
| `.set()` — write + last-write-wins sync | `MergeLastWrite` |
| `.add()` — bump + operation sync, concurrent adds all count | `MergeCrdtSum` |
| key into the JSON state string | field on the Context struct |
| declared ad hoc in code: `SyncVar::user("tap_count")` | declared in a `.vars` sidecar line |

Every SyncVar concept has a Var column waiting for it. The end state is one entity: `Var` gains the runtime behaviour, driven by its markers — `impl Var<T, S, MergeCrdtSum, I>` is where `add()` lives, `MergeLastWrite` is where `set()` lives — so the merge *discipline you declared* is what selects the sync machinery, instead of the caller choosing a method and hoping it matches intent. That's strictly better than today, where nothing stops a feature calling `.set()` on a counter.

Why they can't be literally one type *yet* — and this is a sequencing fact, not a design disagreement: SyncVar's callers live inside composed functions that receive the JSON state string and **have no path to the Context object**. Rung 2 (in flight now) only constructs and holds the Context; nothing is threaded through it. The absorption becomes possible exactly when your original crux lands — composed functions becoming *methods* on Context — because then `self` **is** the context, and `SyncVar::user("tap_count").add(state, 1)` can become `self.counter_count.add(1)` with the value living in the field and the sync op emitted by the marker impl.

So the ladder orders itself:

1. **Rung 2** (running): the Context exists and is observable.
2. **Rung 3**: composed functions become methods — `self` threading, no behaviour change.
3. **Rung 4+**: migrate state out of the JSON string, one feature at a time — each `SyncVar` use becomes a `.vars` declaration and a field access; the broadcast channel starts speaking node-path-keyed var ops; each migrated feature's toggle proof covers both eras.
4. **Last rung**: `SyncVar` has zero callers and is deleted — the merge completes by *absorption*, not by welding two types together mid-flight.

The interim cost of the two-entity state is real but bounded: two names in the crate, with the compiler preventing any confusion between them. Trying to short-circuit it — welding sync methods onto Var while values still live in the JSON string — would hand Var a key-into-JSON identity we'd immediately have to take away again, and reintroduce the scan-the-string world the whole design exists to kill.

I'll write this absorption ladder into the notes entry when I brief rung 3, so the destination is doctrine and not just our chat. Does the sequencing sit right with you — and specifically, are you happy that rung 3 (methods-on-Context) is the next brief after `alive` ships, since it's the enabler for everything else?

Good timing for it — analysis runs in parallel while the worker builds. Let me measure where the seconds actually go before proposing anything:

The numbers reframe the question nicely. A warm link-plus-build on my side is **4.8 seconds** — the local loop is already tight, and deploy itself (rsync + restart + export) adds maybe 15–20s. The real latency budget for ask→shipped is dominated elsewhere:

**Where the minutes actually go** (from the four worker runs: 6.5–14 min each):
1. **Cold cargo builds in worktrees** — the big one. `products/*/build` is generated, so every fresh worktree starts with an empty `target/` and pays full release builds — the server crate *and* the wasm crate with `lto = true, opt-level = "z"` (size-optimised shipping settings) — and pays them *again* for every toggle proof (each untick/re-tick is two full relink+builds). That's plausibly half of each worker's wall time.
2. **Cold-start reading** — just fixed by your persistent-worker idea.
3. **Opus thinking + test rigs** — irreducible in kind, though the persistent worker keeps its node/chrome rigs warm now too.
4. My review + integrate + deploy — small minutes.

**The plan, ranked by impact over effort:**

1. **Shared cargo cache across worktrees** (biggest, cheapest): point `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` at one repo-level shared directory. Cargo handles concurrent access with its own locking, dependency artifacts (serde and friends) compile once ever, and toggle proofs drop from minutes to seconds. Needs zero code changes — it goes into the worker's standing instructions with the rung 5 message.
2. **A dev profile for proof builds**: `lto+opt-z` exists to make the *shipped* wasm small; a toggle proof doesn't need it. A `--quick` flag on fmlink (debug profile, no LTO) for worker proof cycles, with deploy keeping the release profile, cuts each proof cycle further. Small fmlink change — I'll make it between rungs, since the worker owns fmlink territory right now.
3. **The zero-build class** — worth naming because it's the biggest win and it's already on your ladder: once rung 6 lands, a tunable ask ("bigger buttons") is a var edit over sync — *no build, no deploy, seconds to the phone*, with the promotion rule deciding when a constant earns that path. The latency fix for naive asks isn't a faster pipeline; it's leaving the pipeline entirely.
4. Marginal trims I'll take opportunistically: skip the deploy-time feature re-export when no `.md` changed (~4.5s), and overlap my review reading with the worker's final evidence runs.

What I *wouldn't* do: build-on-the-mini (it has no sources by design — that's doctrine), or weaken the toggle-proof discipline to save its build cycles — the proofs are what's keeping this climb correction-free.

> ## Rung 7b — the `counter` merge kind
> 
> A `counter` var holds a `Counter` (epoch + sum). An `add` sums within the current epoch and ships the epoch it was minted under; a `set` opens a new epoch and assigns, so every add still in flight from before it arrives stale and is dropped, loudly. It is the only kind that speaks two verbs, so it is the only one with both `set_at` and `add_at` against its marker and two local entry points (`edit_op` adds, `edit_reset` sets).
> 
> **Evidence** (live, 8097, temporary `tally: Counter = Counter::zero() (global, counter, own)`):
> 
> ```
> 1. A adds +1 and B adds +2, both under epoch 0     tally = [epoch 0, sum 3]
> 2. A resets to 0 — a new epoch opens               tally = [epoch 1, sum 0]
> 3. B's in-flight add, minted under epoch 0         tally = [epoch 1, sum 0]
>    miso: context: .../tally: add of 5 minted under epoch 0 arrived after
>    a reset to epoch 1 — dropped
> 4. adds after the reset sum normally               tally = [epoch 1, sum 10]
> 5. a stale RESET (epoch 0) is dropped too          tally = [epoch 1, sum 10]
> 6. dedupe still holds: {"duplicate":"b3","ok":true} tally = [epoch 1, sum 10]
> 7. the log, compacted:  {"op":"set","value":[1,10],...}   (one line)
>    after restart, replayed from it: [epoch 1, sum 10]
> ```
> 
> **A bug this found in my own 6a work, and fixed.** My first compaction pass folded the counter log to `{"op":"set","value":[0,999]}` — the *stale reset that had been dropped* — because the 6a rule "a set supersedes everything earlier" doesn't know which records were applied and which were dropped. Replay would then have produced `[0,999]` instead of `[1,10]`. The fix is stricter than a patch: **a counter's records are compacted by running `apply_op`'s own rule over them** and emitting the single `set` that lands where replay lands — exact by construction rather than by argument, which is the standard 6a set for itself. Both the broken and the fixed behaviour are in the evidence above.
> 
> **Semantics, argued in `converge.md`:** reset wins, deliberately. A user who presses reset means "from zero, now", and a tap from a moment earlier arriving afterwards to make the counter read 1 is the surprising answer, not the safe one. What changes from SyncVar is not that a race can lose an add — it always could — but that the loss now has a rule, a direction, and a line in the log saying which add went and why. I recorded explicitly that the old behaviour was silently lossy and the new one is deliberately so.
> 
> **Toggle:** there is no node to untick — the vocabulary lives in the family — so the statement is precise instead: with **no counter declared anywhere, the generated source is byte-identical**; the whole delta is 110 lines of the family's own verbatim libraries (the `Counter` type, the marker, the two write impls, the compactor branch), inert until something speaks the word. `edit_reset` is emitted only when a counter exists, which is what makes that true. Tree clean — nothing declares a counter; `tap_count`'s migration is rung 7's.
> 
> **Two things it does not fix**, both in the spec: epochs are minted locally (`self.epoch + 1`), so two racing resets can mint the same number and the later arrival simply wins rather than being recognised as concurrent; and a counter's value type is `Counter`, not `u64`, so readers say `.sum`.

Confirmed on the chains: `… → converge → overlay → payload` on both `update` and `init`. The next node under `converge` inherits the same constraint, which is why it is in the spec rather than only here.

> 1. FIRST PAINT, before any event or flush:   s.motto = "hello"

> 3. the shared LAYER sets it; A has its own:  s.motto = "from A"     (unchanged)
> 4. A clears its override:                    s.motto = "from the layer"
> 5. the layer changes again; the arriving event was ["CtxUpdate"]
>    s.motto = "changed again"    (no extra event needed)

First paint is covered by `init`, not by a server seam: the server never materialises loop state (`boot()` runs `init()` then `render()` in the wasm place), and everything the client learns later arrives as an event, each of which is a turn that republishes on its way out. > `features/miso/loop/context/edit/first-turn/`, extending `boot`. **Measured: 15 full-Context clones per boot → 1.**

> The `Arc` migration, re-enumerated: rung 8 had moved things, so it was **eight** files, not six — `alive.rs`, `per-user.rs`/`.lib.rs`, `remember.rs`/`.lib.rs`, `edit.lib.rs`, and `overlay.rs`/`.lib.rs` (the layer cell is a fifth cell user). Two borrow errors fell out and both were real: a guard taken in a tail expression outliving the handle it borrows.
> 
> **It did not fight the composition machinery** — `Arc&lt;RwLock&lt;Context&gt;&gt;` carries no comma, so the chain signature parses — but it was **not** complete at the Arc: 64.5% returned. The remaining 35% was other people's state, and the fix for it is the part worth reviewing: `/remember` grew a `context_evicted` seam (behaviour-preserving refactor) and `/overlay` hung its own per-user dedupe forgetting on it, because `/remember` cannot call `/overlay` without a backwards dependency. Both maps also hand their buckets back.
> 
> **Rig 6/6, with a counting `GlobalAlloc` patched into the rig binary**: 200 worlds cost **147 KB** (754 bytes each); after the sweep `known`/`resident` return to 2 and **99.9% of the memory comes back** — against **1.2%** with the change reverted, where `known` stayed at 202. An evicted world still rebuilds from its log on the next touch (u7's heartbeat = 7). **RSS does not follow** (4336→4416 KB): that is the system allocator's arena, not memory the server is using, and I say so rather than dressing it up.
> 
> ## S5 — the bridge's complaint (`32286b1`) — built, not parked
> 
> I judged it cheap after finding the key that makes it cheap: **`Context::republish` writes its keys unconditionally, so republishing into an empty object IS the bridged key list** plus this turn's values — no linker change, no second declaration. A key is reported lost when the page's copy differs from what *this mechanism* published there last time (comparing against the context would accuse it of every legitimate change); the complaint rides the payload as `_bridge_lost` and a fragment prints one line per key per load.
> 
> **Rig 2/2**: nothing said when nothing is lost, `['open_tool']` named when the "page" writes it, and silence again once the values agree. **Honest limit**: the Rust half is proven; the `console.warn` itself was not observed firing, because my rig has no JS-eval channel — the fragment is composed, gated by `/obey`, and inspected only statically. **Known noise, named in the spec**: `/seamless` restores a whole state object across an update, so it will complain once per bridged key after a seamless upgrade — technically true complaints, left loud rather than special-cased.
> 
> ## Full regression, final composition
> 
> **57 checks, 0 failed**, plus the turn probe: rig5 the done-sentence 8/8 (untick → tool leaves → never-seen device agrees → different person untouched → survives restart → re-tick restores with the count at 3 → counts to 4), rig4 fragment gates 14/14, rig6 self-untick 4/4, rig7 same-door 7/7, rig8 sole-tenant 5/5, rig9 unmixed 5/5, rig10 one-broadcast 6/6, rig11 eviction 6/6, rig12 bridge 2/2. Release `build OK`. Coverage now 71 of 122 nodes gating something at runtime; the tree is clean and 8095 was never touched.
> 
> ## Open risks
> 
> - **`first-turn` changes what a gate reads during boot** from "the live world, freshly cloned each time" to "the frozen view plus this turn's own mirrored writes". Those agree by construction (edits mirror), and the only difference is that a foreign edit landing mid-boot is now invisible — the boundary law working — but it is a semantic change, not just a saving.
> - **Eviction now removes the table entry**, so a request already holding a handle finishes against a world that has been emptied. Its writes still reach the log and the next touch rebuilds; the window is a user idle past the threshold whose request arrives during the sweep, and `except` excludes the requesting user.
> - **`context_evicted` is a seam with a rule** ("must be rebuildable from the log"). It is enforced by prose, not by types.
> - **S5's console line is unobserved** (above), and its seamless-upgrade noise is by choice.
> - **`_bridge_lost` adds a state key** on the paints where something was lost; it is removed when there is nothing to say, so it cannot go stale, but it is one more key fragments could trip over.
>
